utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you understand, do you, you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you made last week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Oh, yes. I think we're in to you, Mr. Domazet. The pseudonym sheet will be put before the witness. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I start the cross-examination, with the Court's indulgence, may I state that instead of Mr. Tanaskovic, who is absent, that you allow Mr. Bosko Ristic, legal counsel and attorney from Nis, to assist me here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you something about what you said about leaving Visegrad at the beginning of April 1992. You said that on the 4th or 5th of April you had to leave Visegrad. I am not quite clear as to the reasons. Were the reasons because of the threats or your official duty which you had to perform in Medzedza. Could you clear that up, please.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both reasons. The first reason was that I was assigned to that part of the terrain. It was my duty to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you talk about Medzedza, could you explain to us whether there was a police station there.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you mean a separate building or premises where this police station was located?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station was located in a socially owned building, in a room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from you, were there other policemen on duty there at that time?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One or more?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a reserve police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it was set up as a reserve police station; is that right, at that time, or had it been established quite a long time before that?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was established quite a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, when it was established?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exact date of the establishment, following a decree by the Minister for Internal Affairs Bosnia-Herzegovina was the 21st of April, 1991. That is the official date. I apologise. May I just add: I think I said April, but it was the 21st of September. The 21st of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for the formation of that police station at that time?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was a decree, an order from the Internal Affairs Minister of the country, and the reason is common knowledge. A police station existed previously for 10 or 15 years as a reserve police station, because I was the commandeer of that station for some time and it was activated exactly on the 21st of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that it was pursuant to an order from the Minister, but what I was asking you was: Do you know the precise reason why that reserve police station was formed precisely on that date, the 21st of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, [redacted] [redacted] that was once again reactivated after a certain period of time, but you weren't actually told why it was being reactivated at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. We had our regular duties and assignments, the general type of thing that the police force does, general police duties. And may I add something: It wasn't only that police station which was activated, but eight other reserve police stations on the territory of the Visegrad municipality, and predominantly in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think all these police stations were activated, reactivated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you. That's what I want to know. You've just given me a partial answer. What I'm asking you is: This reactivation of the police stations, was that due to the general situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina or a state of emergency on the Visegrad territory?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a state of emergency in this area and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so there were these extraordinary circumstances prevailing in Visegrad too and the territory around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Domazet. Sir, because you and Mr. Domazet are both speaking the same language, you make it difficult for the interpreters unless there is a break after the question before you answer. Mr. Domazet, you may have noticed, is pausing before he asks you the question. That's to enable the interpreters to catch up. We are receiving it in English and in French, so that you should just wait just a few moments to enable them to catch up. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, [redacted] of that reserve police station in Medzedza, did the exodus of the Serb population from Visegrad and its environs start then?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The departure of the Serb population from Visegrad -- well, I don't know whether it took place, but I do know, and we're talking about the month of April -- actually, March, the beginning of April, before the entry of the Romanija and Uzice corps into parts of the Visegrad municipality from Medzedza, in view of the fact that in Medzedza there were three Serb houses, but the households left and went to Visegrad from the Medzedza area. Now, if you want the name and surname of these people, I can tell you them. May I just add something, please. One of those families, one of the families that left from Visegrad, the son came of that mother - the name is Furtula, Milka Furtula, and he was the commander of the Romanija corps and he took her away, his mother away, and the others before the corps actually entered, that is to say, a few days before the corps' arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it was from that time on that Medzedza was exclusively populated by the Muslim population; is that right? There were no more Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There were no more Serbs in Medzedza. But there were some Serbs in the environs. They all lived quite normally in their houses and worked, went about their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Prior to your departure from Visegrad at the beginning of April 1992, were there any incidents with any victims, involving any victims? Had somebody already been killed at that time? Were there casualties?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And let me add. Let me give you an explanation. Round the clock, non-stop, almost every day, I was in the Medzedza area and I would go home only sporadically from time to time, so that I don't know what actually happened in town. I don't want to make any statements along those lines. What I'm saying now, please, I would like to have recorded. I want to have it in the record. I was in charge of the upper part of the terrain, and for two weeks I didn't know when it was day, when it was night. I had so many duties to perform. I was on duty round the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. What I was asking you was about the period up to your departure, prior to your departure, were there any incidents like that?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I didn't see anything like that. Mr. Domazet, I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But sir, when you say that you had such a lot of work to do in Medzedza, day and night, that you couldn't have a breather, that Medzedza at that time was exclusively populated by Muslims, what problems could you have had, then, in a village for you to have had so much work to do, as you say, round the clock, non-stop?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence counsel, 74 square kilometres is the local community of Medzedza, with 1.556 inhabitants, and it was enough for me just to tour the area, and seven days would not have been enough for me to go around that area, let alone do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told me that you don't remember, up until your departure from Visegrad, whether there were any victims, any casualties. Do you remember that a Serb from Visegrad by the name of Indzic was killed?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't killed during those days, but I heard later on in Medzedza that Indzic had been killed. I don't know his first name. But I know that he was somewhere from my neighbourhood. He lived somewhere in the neighbourhood of Pionirska Street in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that he was shot at from the direction of your house?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me ask you once again: Did that killing perhaps not take place -- the killing of Indzic, was that not perhaps the reason why you left Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I said that I would go from time to time into Visegrad to take a bath, have a change of clothes, from Medzedza, because the police station was up there, so I had to stay there. And that is not the reason, what you've just said is not the reason for my leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I think you said that after your departure on the 4th or 5th of April, you never returned to Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I didn't go home to Visegrad because the Romanija corps was to enter from the Rogatica direction into Medzedza, so I was in the field, in the terrain, so I didn't have time to come back ever again. And the reason that I didn't come back was more because I had received threats and because my people, or let me say my late wife, told me that they were looking for me and looking for all progressive Muslims in Visegrad, that the Serb police were arresting them and the paramilitary, that they were searching the houses, going -- doing house searches, that they were calling people up by phone and generally bothering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In a previous statement that you made, you said, sir, that your brother had informed you that you -- they were looking for you in Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have some contacts with my brother and the rest of my family whenever I could, not only with my wife, and I also contacted the police station and the police chief there, the head, and the other people to whom I was subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But what I asked you was: Do you remember your brother warning you that they were looking for you?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As I understand it, your immediate family and that brother of yours stayed on in Visegrad and were actually in Visegrad at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the local inhabitants of Visegrad were in Visegrad until Murat released the water from the dam, the hydro power plant, and until the Uzice corps entered town. I can't say whether all of them stayed, but I do know some citizens who left Visegrad previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From the information that you got, you therefore learnt that many had left the town because of Murat's threat to raise the dam and release the water down the Drina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murat stated publicly, made a public announcement that he would release the water from the dam, and the people from the surrounding parts around the lake, whose houses were below the level of the hydro power plant left. I wasn't in town to see that taking place, but by what I heard from the people who talked about it and who came into the Medzedza area, and those who left for Gorazde, I heard that some went to Uzamnica, to the barracks there. Others went to the village of Medzedza and the surrounding villages where the water would not have reached the land to flood it had it been released from the dam. And there was general panic in town at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Up until the arrival of the Uzice corps, which was on the 13th of April, 1992, if I'm right, the chief of police in Visegrad was Ilijas Suceska. That's what you said. He was a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, prior to the arrival of the corps and your departure, were there Serb policemen in the Visegrad police station or had they already left?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in town there were Serbs there too in the police administration in Visegrad. Let me state the following: Mr. Dragan Tomic was a higher-ranking inspector in that police station. Mr. Sredoje Lukic was a policeman at the police station. Niko Vujcic and others. I don't want to enumerate them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know or did you hear that at that period after your departure from Visegrad and before the arrival of the Uzice Corps, a group of those particular policemen had been arrested and detained, taken into custody, amongst them the men you mentioned, Sredoje Lukic a case in point?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the exact date when this happened, what the exact date was when they were arrested, but I do know that they were arrested, yes. That is to say, I heard about it, I didn't actually see it taking place. But let me be precise and specific and state here and now from this seat that my first meeting with my former colleagues was -- I can't quite remember exactly whether it was the 14th of April or the 15th of April, towards evening. And I released 13 prisoners in Medzedza. I ensured a kombi van for them [redacted] of the reserve police station, Hurian [phoen] Nedjib and Ibrahim Hurian [phoen] took those 13 prisoners to the hydro power plant of Visegrad, which had been taken over by the army and paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but those 13 people, that has nothing to do with the group I was asking you about, talking about. It wasn't Sredoje Lukic and others.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. All the people that I mentioned. There were my colleague Sredo Lukic, Niko Vujicic, and a man named Dragicevic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that that group, including Sredo Lukic and the other policemen who had been arrested and who were at the power plant -- I'm not sure that I understood you properly. Did they pass through Medzedza? Were they where you were at the station, or what?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The same day they came to Medzedza, I think it was the 14th, the first day the Uzice Corps entered Visegrad, the 14th of April, towards evening. I learnt in Medzedza that that group allegedly who had been taken prisoner was taken to Medzedza, this group of prisoners, taken to Medzedza and they were put up in the house of Hamed Sisic, from Medzedza, right next to the lake, right by the lake. I went there, as I have already said, towards evening. I called Mr. Sredoje to come out and told him the reason I would be coming with a vehicle, that they should be prepared and that I was going to take them back home to Visegrad, which I did indeed do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I follow you, what you did was you finally released that group and let them go back home to Visegrad; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how many days they were in custody?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that at that hydro electric power plant they were detained in some other place?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I didn't spend any time in Visegrad during those few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite clear that you weren't there. You said that. But I thought that perhaps somebody, or them, had told you about that. That's why I'm asking you. But if you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence counsel, let me tell you: Here and now, sitting here, I am just telling you of things I'm certain about and that I can confirm at any time, whenever asked, and I think that Their Honours and the Prosecution and everybody else present here in the courtroom must know that when the whole town went out in a panic, thousands of people, women and children, can you imagine what kind of situation that was, when nobody was in their houses any more, when they were not normal any more? It was general pandemonium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were the person who saw these men and who released them and maybe spoke to some of them, my question is: How did they look, physically? Did they look like people who had been mistreated, beaten up, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to anyone. My sole contact was with Sredo Lukic and it was a brief contact. The man appeared to be terrified. He wasn't a normal person. And my colleagues called me by my nickname, [redacted]. So during that first contact of mine with Sredoje, I said, "What happened to you?" And the man said, "You see what happened." That was the whole conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Had you noticed that all of them, including Sredoje that you spoke to, had had their heads shaved?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the others. I only saw Sredoje, and Sredoje did have his head shaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't see the others, I assume that you didn't talk to them, but physically, surely, you must have seen them.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said to Lukic that in half an hour this assistant of mine would be arriving, the one who was working with me at the time, that he would bring a vehicle and that they should go out the western side, where no one can see them, to get into the van and to be taken home, and that is what happened. But I didn't go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move on to another subject, that is, the event that you described during your examination-in-chief, and that is the event of the 13th or 14th of June, as you said, according to what your father told you. You have given us quite a lot of detail and I will ask you a few questions regarding those details, if you can to tell us, as you also mentioned these things in your previous statements. You mentioned probably on the basis of what your father told you, that the column that was going to Visegrad was joined by a person called Milorad Mico Lipovac, if I'm not mistaken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said that Mico Lipovac, Micun, known as Micun, approached the column in a location called Greben, where he lives. At least, that is what my father told me. Whether he reached the town, I don't know, because I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that in your earlier statements you said that, because of exhaustion, Saha Uspahic decided not to continue along the road to Visegrad? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A bus came along which was transporting other citizens that had been expelled from remote places and it caught up with Saha, who got into the bus. It was packed full, so the bus couldn't take anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, on the basis of the stories that people told you, what day of the week was it when they reached Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I do know that it was the fourth day of the Bajram, the Muslim holiday, what we call the Kurban Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that that same day was also a rather important Orthodox holiday?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were describing what was happening in Visegrad that day, according to the source that you had, you spoke about two separate incidents. So will you please listen to me and confirm whether what I am saying is right. The first around 1400 hours. The time doesn't matter so much, but just so as to know what we're talking about. That first event, according to what you said, Mitar Vasiljevic, Sredoje Lukic and Milan Lukic take people to Pionirska Street whereas the others were nearby; Djuric, Krsmanovic, Susnjar and Ilic, and at that time they were looted by this first group. And the second incident, which you said occurred in the evening, about 2200 to 2300 hours, when they continued the search and then the house was set on fire. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me correctly, but if that is what I said, I need to make a correction. Around 1400 hours, they were brought in front of the house and told them that they shouldn't move from that house. They got into the house, and those who were present I listed before, and they were in the immediate vicinity of the house. And about 1400 hours, according to what my father said, 1600 hours, yes, they searched the house, took the money and jewellery and everything they took, and then, around 2200 hours - I'm not quite sure about the time - they appeared again and they are the ones that I listed before. They appeared in the house, and after that, they again started the search and chasing people out of that house and forcing them into the other house, next to the creek where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So I think that the only clarification or correction that you made -- but I was relying on the transcript -- now you are saying that there were three incidents, one about 1400 hours, when they reached Pionirska Street, the second at 1600 hours, when they were searched and looted, and the third in the evening, when the search was continued and they were taken to another house where they were set on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make myself clear. You are making -- leading me into a contradiction, which I would like to avoid. I said that around 1400 hours, but I'm not quite sure. It could be plus, minus something, because my father didn't tell me explicitly. Anyway, these victims that are on this list, and others, were brought, around 1400 hours, from the Liberation Square - that is, one and a half kilometres away from the site of the event - and they were escorted by Mitar Vasiljevic, carrying an automatic rifle and firing into the air, and they were told that no one may leave the house. And then, after 14 -- after 16, around 1600 hours -- you as a lawyer, you must know, you must realise that I can't be specific. I'm saying around 1600 hours. These mentioned people came, they took the money, jewellery, gold and went in the direction of Bikovac, where probably they had an orgy, because when they came again, they were all drunk. And this event, as I said, occurred sometime around 2400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Now you've explained about the time. I didn't say 1600. I said around 1600, and I quite accept what you're telling us, and it is up to this Trial Chamber to establish what exactly happened and when. When you went on to describe that evening and the taking of the people to the Omeragic house, the house close to the creek where the fire occurred, you explained that your father was among the last, if not the last, to be pushed into that room where some people were already located.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the last to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also spoke about the windows in that room. How do you know what those windows looked like?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from what my father said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. And also from what he said when the explosion occurred, the door blew open, and since his legs were not hurt, he got out and headed downhill towards the creek below the house; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said he rolled down the slope to the creek, which is about 20 or 30 metres away, and that is how he entered a mound of cornstalks. I think I explained exactly what I meant in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but I was talking about the direction, though. Did he walk for a while and then roll down? But in any event, from the door of the house, he went down to the creek, downhill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he saw anyone at all at that moment?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At this part of the cornstalks, he stayed there all day, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, hidden behind these stalks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you told us here in court, you learnt about this event first from Witness VG13.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that this was about ten days or so after the event.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Don't hold me to my word whether it was nine, ten or eleven days, or eight days, but ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you said, for some 20 years you were a policeman, when you were talking about your professional career.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if you're interested, I can give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. This tells me that you had a lot of experience and that you were an experienced policeman. I think that would be right to say of a man who was in that profession for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, in view of the fact that this was part of the police duties, do you remember the provisions of Rule 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure? May I remind you perhaps, if that would help?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do help me. I can't remember it just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is a provision of the Law on Criminal Procedure authorising official persons of MUP to take statements and interview witnesses which later cannot be used in evidence in court but are used in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Pursuant to that provision of the law, did you take a statement from Witness VG13 in the police station in Medzedza?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had no opportunity to do it. The witness was wounded and went on for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you said that you had one conversation with this witness when she -- when the witness said that your immediate family was not involved, that they had left for Olovo, and then two days later the same person told you that your family had died; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So we are talking of a period of at least three days of this person being in Medzedza, if not longer, so how can you say, then, that you didn't have time to interview this person for such an important event as the killing of a large number of people?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you realise, Defence counsel, that it was an emergency and a wartime situation? Do you know that? Please answer my question before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will tell you, though I am not here to give answers - you are here to answer questions - but I will tell you that I do know what the situation was like but that, as a lawyer, I really do not understand how a policeman with 20 years of experience who learns of such a terrible criminal offence does not take a statement from a witness who later could have got killed and been unable to testify ever. So I must say that I find that strange on your part, being an experienced policeman.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I have said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If that is true, do you remember, sir, that in the statement that you made just over a year ago to the investigator of the OTP here from The Hague, you did not mention at all that VG13 had given you any information about this in Medzedza but you said that you learnt about it on the basis of telephone conversations with people from Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not right. You have my statement where this witness is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you very specifically: In your statement to the investigator, is it true that you said that you learnt about the event from telephone conversations with people in Visegrad and not from this witness, whom you did not mention at all in your statement as a source of information about this event?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not -- it is not correct that I said that I learnt by telephone. If I did say so, there's a correction. I learnt for the first time about this event from the witness, using this number that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that it was extremely important to tell the investigator whom you had learnt about such an event from?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every event is very important for the investigation and the Court, every detail, but I must express a reservation: If I did not tell the investigator during the last statement in Sarajevo, let them look for my first statement which I made to the investigator. I think that this witness number 13 is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many times did you give statements to the investigator of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was twice or three times. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you including statements to the MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina or only the investigator from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the investigator from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me remind you. I'm referring to your statement of May 2000 and the investigator is Ib Jul Hansen. Do you remember making a statement for him?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Allow me to read a part of that statement to refresh your memory, and it refers to what we have just discussed. You said, and I quote: "The telephone lines between the town and Medzedza were open for at least another month after I had left Visegrad. Occasionally I spoke to relatives in Visegrad, not openly, because I suspected that the Serbs were listening in to the telephone conversations; however, in one way or another I was informed about the situation over there. They told me about a fire in a house in Pionirska Street on the 13th or 14th of June, 1992, when 64 people died. The owner of the house was Adem Omeragic. My father --" I won't mention his name for your protection, and some other -- "and a number of others survived this. I know of another two survivors." And the names are given, and these are witnesses 13 and 18. And you know very well who they are. And let me go on: "I was told that the fire or explosion had occurred because fire was opened at the house from a hand-held rocket launcher. My father also told me who the people who did this were, and they were," and you then go on to mention the names. Do you remember giving such a statement to investigator Hansen?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but information can be obtained in one way or another; I think that is quite clear. You are a lawyer, so you must know how one gets information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this is what you said in that statement, and in that statement you did not mention a conversation with Witness VG13 in Medzedza or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you left that out, but that is why I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but for the credibility of a statement of a witness, it is very important what he said and when, and that is why I'm asking you these questions.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but it's ten years since I left my home. I hardly know my own name any more. And let me add that in this war I lost nine close relatives, Mr. Defence Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, believe me that I'm fully conscious of the situation and I am very sorry that you have lost so many members of your family. I commiserate. That is very unfortunate and sad. But you must also understand that, regardless of that, it is very important to tell the truth, the whole truth, so that the real culprits, if that is possible, be brought before justice. That is the aim of the Trial Chamber, of the Tribunal, and me as Defence counsel, and I hope that you, as a man who dealt with this kind of thing, understand that, although the period which was for you personally very difficult will be able to understand our endeavours and why, precisely why we were trying to get at the truth.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, when you spoke about the persons who were in the column moving towards Visegrad that day [Technical difficulty], members of your immediate and larger family, you said that in addition to them, [Technical difficulty] whom you knew and that you met them often and came into contact with them often, [Technical difficulty] the statement of your interview, the minutes of your interview. Can you remember who these other people were? And I think you have a list in front of you with their names.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One moment. We're getting French as well as English at the moment. I'm not sure -- it's not continuous, but it's certainly coming in and out often. Very pleasant to hear, but confusing.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Mr. President, if it's my fault. Shall we move one of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, sir. That is to make sure they catch you no matter which way you're looking. It's not your microphone, but let's proceed and see if it's fixed, Mr. Domazet. I'm sorry, the witness was about to start answering. He said, "Yes, I can tell you ..." You proceed now, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victims, I think that you have a list of their names. Do you want me to give you their names and surnames? And I can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there would be any harm in you giving us the names of the people who weren't part of your family whom you mentioned and who are on the list and who you say you knew and met.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Redzo Memisevic and Fazila Memisevic, they are neighbours of mine from the same village. Number 36, victim number 36, Mule Ajanovic, is also a neighbour, a lady neighbour of mine from my village. Kada Sehic and Faruk Sehic, from the village of Musici. My sister and my sister's son. Then there was Velic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, sir. I think you already told us that. You told us those names already and you told us during your testimony and examination. But you spoke about some others as well.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence Counsel, please, may I take it in order and clear this up. That's why I'm here. Nurka Velic, Tima Velic from Sase. Because the proceedings were interrupted, there was a correction made to the surname of the victims under number 48 and 49 and 50. It was not Jasarevic. That was not the surname. It was [redacted]. And there was one person omitted, that is to say, two victims which were left out of the list, with no number. They would be after -- they would be number 52 and 53. And one of these people, the surname is [redacted], the first name is Rabija. The number is 52, she is under number 52. And number 53 is Ajnija Delija. That is a woman. Ajnija Delija, and I'd like that to be entered into the record with the number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The list you've been reading from, which is Exhibit P147, did you compile the list or was it compiled according to what you said or were you given it by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was given to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking about individuals under 48, 49, and 50, you said there was an error in their surname. When did you discover that error?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just when the proceedings were interrupted last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that after the interruption, after your testimony was interrupted, you had contacts with other witnesses. Perhaps some of those witnesses told you about that change, or did you really notice it yourself and notice that it was -- that they were other names?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the other witnesses told me, because I know each of these individuals personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So number 48 is [redacted]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the village of Sase. And if the President of the Court will allow me, may I add one more name to this list, which I have just remembered? The person's name is Jasarevic. I don't know the first name exactly, but I think her name was Razija, and she joined the column later, or them. And she disappeared as of that date. All trace of her is lost. She was Zarfa Jasarevic. She was between the ages -- she might have been 50 or 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, there was one Jasarevic, and that is the one you've just told us about. The others aren't Jasarevic but [redacted]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what I understood, you knew [redacted] personally.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about him, any particulars; where he worked, where he lived, who he lived with, things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. You've told us enough, so you know him well and you know that his wife survived and that she is still living; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So according to you, she wasn't in Pionirska Street on that particular critical day.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Although you were quite specific in saying that there was only one Jasarevic, the man you just remember -- the person you just remembered, can I just ask you if there was anybody called (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: (redacted) except that person Zarfa, the last one, under number 54, the woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Referring to the statement you gave to the investigator of the Prosecution, Mr. Hansen, and the introductory part that I read out to you which you said was correct and true, that you did in fact say that, you gave us an explanation with respect to how you learnt about this, but you didn't tell me why you mentioned a hand-held rocket launcher as the way in which the fire was created. And here, in this court, you described this in quite a different way.

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what my father said. My father said that it was probably a hand-held rocket launcher, which was seen at 2400 hours in a closed room with no light. But as he was an elderly person and had experienced two world wars, he probably knew that it was a strong weapon of great destructive power, and according to what he said, he thought it was a hand-held rocket launcher, that that would correspond to the type of weapon used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Your father did make a statement. It was recorded. I hope we shall see that, a recording of that. But thank you anyway. We have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is taking the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: One question, VG61: Were you specifically asked by the investigator about any conversations with the surviving victims, VG13, the other surviving victim being VG18?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So you were only specifically asked to recount what your father told you; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VG61 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, VG61.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: That would conclude the re-examination. However, I would like to officially tender the videotape. A clip of it was shown last Wednesday. And the transcripts in English and B/C/S into evidence, which is Prosecution Exhibits marked 145 is the videotape, 146.1 the English translation, 146.2 the B/C/S translation, all being handed out just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any objection to this, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no objection. But in view of the answers given by the witness, I think that it would be necessary for the Prosecution to agree and confirm the fact that the witness, in a statement to investigator Hansen, made no mention of his talk with Witness VG13 and that, in the way that I described, he did testify, without having to tender that statement of his into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We can agree that it is not recorded in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now, Exhibits 146.1 and 146.2, with the prefix P, are admitted and they are under seal. What about the video? I don't remember, did that identify anybody?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It's 145. A clip was apparently, according to the record - I was not in court unfortunately, so I didn't see it - but a clip was shown and I think the tape, the original tape, is with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was definitely shown. My only concern was, was it shown in private session? We can look it up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to recall that we just saw the first ten seconds of that tape, for the witness to identify his father, which he did do, and after that, we agreed that the video clip be shown after this examination, so that it was not shown, in fact, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that part which was shown clearly must have been shown in private session, because it would have identified the witness. Well, then it too will be under seal. It's Exhibit P145. But what about showing us the whole of it? I must say, unless it's of some importance - and very few videos have been of any importance so far - we might be able to miss that. It's all very well to show them because --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I think basically everything that we needed to be recorded is recorded in the transcript, so I mean if Your Honours don't wish to see it, I don't think that we insist on watching the whole video in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. We will note that the first ten seconds was shown. That's the only part which is relevant, which identifies the witness's father, and we don't need to have regard to the rest of it. Is there some problem with that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that regardless of the fact that we do indeed have a transcript, both in English and B/C/S, of that interview, that it would be a good idea - it's not a long one, some ten minutes perhaps - to show it. For the Court to be able to assess what the witness has said, I think that would be necessary. And that is the -- I think that was Mr. Groome's proposal too, but we put it off for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would guess that the video does not have an English sound track; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: That's correct. There is an English transcript of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what we have in Exhibit 146, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And I think the whole transcript of the whole videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I find it very difficult to read a transcript and to watch a video at the same time, which means in the end that the interpreters are going to have to give us an interpretation. Do you know about the length of time? Was ten minutes a fair estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It could be about right. I mean, I think the whole transcript is reflected, the whole transcript of his interview about the incidents, but I personally must confess I haven't stopped it and I don't have a copy here now to see whether there is an indication of timing on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we ask the booth whether they feel prepared to, with the assistance of the transcript, interpret --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, if we have a transcript, if we're given a copy of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got a copy, a spare copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we gave our spare copy to the Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll let them have the exhibit. It's very easy. We've got copies. And has the video booth got the tape? And we will have to go into private session for the purposes of hearing it. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're now in public session. The estimate was a little out, I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet, but thank you. Thank you also to the people in the booth and the court reporters for staying on. Well, sir, that concludes your part in these proceedings. We're very grateful to you to having come and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave. We will adjourn now and resume again at 5 to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President. I have a request, if I may. Could I ask you, Your Honours, the Defence counsel, and the accused, if they know, and they know where the graves are, to help me to bury my family, if I could find a bone somewhere, to bury my family and friends. That's all for now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, that is something which is often raised here in court. I am afraid that the Tribunal generally is unable to assist you. There is, of course, a great deal of information being given to us. We have the next witness -- I'm sorry, the next witness but one has had a lot to do with finding bodies, but I'm sure that so far as the Prosecution is concerned, which has access to that material, they will give you what they have, but I don't think that it is appropriate to call upon the Defence in the trial. We have no basis upon which we could say that they know the answer to it. To do otherwise would be to assume their guilt, which would not be proper for us. But I hope, sir, that you find the bodies of your family. As I say, you are now free to leave and we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ossogo. Please stand up, sir. Would you take the solemn declaration in the document which the Court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is witness who will have the pseudonym VG21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got a pseudonym sheet for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President; document number 80, Prosecution document 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P80, 8-0, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness VG21, the piece of paper that you have before you contains some information. Is the information, the particulars, correct on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I should just like to tell you that any information concerning family ties should not be mentioned in the course of your testimony and the relationship that links -- you can tell us the relationship that links you to those persons, but don't say their names, please. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The same thing applies to the village that is mentioned at the end of the piece of paper. You will just say, "A," when you refer to the village in the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In 1992, Witness VG21, you lived in Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In village A; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And you completed your compulsory military service in the JNA in 1965?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Up until what year? How long did you do your military service for? Until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: From 1965 to 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You were a soldier in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In 1992, did you leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What month was that, precisely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, 1992. That is to say, the 19th of May. I apologise. I misspoke. The 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you leave Visegrad before the month of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I left when the Uzice Corps arrived. I went off in the direction of Gorazde before the Uzice Corps entered, and that was in April, the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you left the town of Visegrad on the 14th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Because it was rumoured that the Uzice Corps was coming and entering the town of Visegrad. However, the man who released the water, for security reasons I left, not knowing what was going to happen in that town of ours, the town of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said the man who released the water. Which man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: His name was Murat Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And who released what water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. It was the lake of the hydro electric power plant of Visegrad and it was on the river Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was it because you were afraid of flooding, that the city would be flooded? Is that why you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How long did you stay away for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I was absent for nine days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: En route, did you come across any checkpoints or control points, if you prefer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: You mean when I was leaving or when I returned? On my way back or on my way out?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Going away and coming back nine days later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: When I left, there were no barricades or checkpoints until Gorazde, and upon my return, when the Uzice Corps had entered, I think it was the 14th of April, perhaps a day before or a day afterwards - I can't quite remember the date at which the corps entered Visegrad precisely - but nine days later, the Uzice Corps had set up entrance controls or checkpoints, checkpoints at the entrance to the town of Visegrad, in different places, at different entrances, 200 metres apart or half a kilometre or one kilometre apart, at all the junctions leading into town, into the settlement, or exits from the settlements, including the town of Visegrad itself. In the town itself, at every 200 metres, there were checkpoints. Your personal documents were checked and people were checked as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: May we take it, then, that these checkpoints were placed when you left and when you returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I said I saw checkpoints set up on my journey back from Gorazde to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you yourself checked? Did they search you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What did this control or check consist of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: It was the legal arm of the Yugoslav People's Army, regular soldiers, in the presence of the reserve force, the reserve units. Whether they were paramilitary or whether they were the legal units of the legal army, I'm not sure. They were called the reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: To go back to the distinction that you make between regular soldiers and reservists, how were the other people checked and how was the control effected of the other people, if you happened to see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Ramps were set up, manned by several soldiers or a group of soldiers, and they would stop people, stop the people coming back, pedestrians or cars, people coming in on foot or by car. They would be stopped at these checkpoints and they asked them to show their ID documents, and if anybody had any weapons, ranging from knives to rifles, they asked people whether they were armed, and anything they suspected might be interesting for military purposes and strategy. If they thought this was so, they would confiscate these items. If they found a knife on someone or a pistol on someone or binoculars or various other equipment, they would confiscate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: At that particular time, was there a distinction between -- did they distinguish between the people they checked and controlled based on ethnicity, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. They only did this on an ethnic basis. They searched the Bosniak population mostly, of the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How were the soldiers dressed, the ones you mentioned, the ones who manned the checkpoints and did the checking? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: They wore the uniform, the olive-green/grey uniform of the former Yugoslav People's Army, that kind of uniform, and everything that went with it, and also the kind of uniform that regular soldiers had and everything that went with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You also mentioned reservists. Did they wear the same type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, they did, the only difference being that the reservists could be distinguished from the others, from the regular soldiers of the JNA. They didn't have caps of any kind. They didn't have the Tito-type caps and emblems on their heads. That was the difference. And their uniforms were like the ones that regular soldiers had, the soldiers serving the former army, the JNA. The uniform that the reservists had could be noted for its -- whether it was clean or whether it was dirty, whether -- that is to say, you could tell who were irregular soldiers who had joined the reservists. Their uniforms tended to be dirty and torn, so you could notice that some of these uniforms were dirty and torn as opposed to the other clean ones. They were also not well kept, not combed. They had beards, they weren't clean-shaven, and their conduct was different as well. They behaved differently towards the people they were checking. Their demeanour was different. They would curse the people, they would swear, and there was a lot of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples of that mistreatment that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They would usually swear, curse their balija mothers or Turkish mothers and use derogatory terms. And they would ask, "Where is Murat and what do you think is going to happen to you now?" They would say that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those insults meant, swearing your balija mother and your Turkish mother? Did that signify anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. Cursing balijas is a sort of extreme -- something extreme or a special crime, like we used to use the terms "Chetnik" or "Ustasha," that kind of meaning. Because there were quite a lot of them, a lot of them who personally knew the man whose name and surname -- that is to say, they would know people by their first and last names but they would nonetheless refer to them as balijas or Turks or that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you came back after spending nine days in Gorazde, when you came back to your village, was your property intact or had anybody been to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: When I returned from Gorazde, what I found was the house in which I live, it was intact. Nobody had touched it. There were no changes. It was in the same state as I had left it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you were in your house after your return, did a group of soldiers come and visit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. When I went into the house - I can't say exactly, but about 20 minutes later or half an hour later maybe, a patrol of the Yugoslav People's Army came in with four soldiers, and they were stationed in the barracks at Uzamnica, the Uzamnica barracks under the command of Dragan Burandzic, the commander of that particular unit. The soldiers who came to search my house at first behaved decently; their conduct was proper. They searched my house and the premises. They did not find anything -- any of the kinds of things that they were looking for, or asked me if I had, such as weapons or -- actually, they weren't looking for anything else. That's what they were looking for, just weapons. They did ask me whom I had, who was in the house with me and who my family were, what family members I had. I told them that my wife and daughter were with me, and that's all I had to do with those soldiers. I had no problems any more that day with the soldiers. I'm thinking about the people who came from the barracks, the Uzamnica barracks. Not half an hour went by after that when an army patrol came by again. They didn't introduce themselves, say who they were, but there were two of them. They were very nicely dressed, and three other men were reservists. And I recognised a neighbour of mine who also mistreated me in the presence of those five soldiers. He was looking -- he wanted me -- he was looking for a pistol or a rifle that I might have, and ammunition. They searched the house, ransacking it, looking everywhere, just like the group before them did. They found nothing. He saw a picture I had on the wall, and it was a photograph of Josip Broz, Tito. He said, "Do you still believe --" and I apologise for using these words -- "in this shit? And fuck you if you do." He took the photograph and smashed it right in front of my very eyes in my own home, and he said that I could forfeit my head for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes. Just one moment, please, Witness VG21. Did the soldiers take any property that belonged to you, movable goods or not, that second group that came half an hour after the first group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No. The third group did. After that, the next day, they came again. They would spend half an hour, sometimes more, sometimes less. You didn't know who was coming after that, who was looking for what, and if you got your house in order, if you tidied up, if they found your house tidy, they would ransack it even more. If your house wasn't all tidy and if you had left it in a shambles, the way it was when they ransacked it, they would upset you less; they would do less. I was there, actually. It was only if they took a liking to something or saw some cigarettes or some technical goods, for example, that they could take off with them and nobody would notice, then they took those, some carpentry equipment. Because I had my tools, my carpentry tools, and they took all my tools with them. They took anything they liked, they took a fancy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said they took everything. Can you tell us what they took, apart from your carpentry tools?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: They took a carton of cigarettes belonging to my son, they took three machines, carpentry machines, because he was a carpenter, had done his training in Visegrad; they took my own tools from my vehicle, the tools I used every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When did the Uzice Corps leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: As far as I know and am able to remember, I think it was the 19th of May, in the evening, or in the night between the 18th and 19th of May, as far as I remember, but possibly it could have been a day earlier or a day later, give or take a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After the departure of the Uzice Corps, did you notice any paramilitary units in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. Those groups were stationed, that is to say, they were put up at the new Visegrad hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which group are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the paramilitary groups, the White Eagles or Seselj's men or Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were they housed in a particular building, the White Eagles, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: That is to say, were they in different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. They wore civilian uniforms, the olive-green/grey uniforms, they had caps, the French beret type of cap, they had white coats on, white overalls. They were dressed differently. Some had long coats on, winter coats on, military boots but civilian clothing. So there were all kinds of combinations and different types of uniforms. Those paramilitary units wore all sorts of different clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them had rifles, pistols, and a bomb or two, a grenade or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Your brother-in-law, was he the object of a visit by one of these groups? Did they visit your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which group went to your brother-in-law's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: It was the White Eagles group belonging to Dragan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When they went to see him, did they do anything in particular, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Dragan Lukic took a Passat type car from Dzemo Zukic. Dzemo Zukic was the owner of the vehicle. And he drove it to the NK22 [as interpreted], stopped, and below his house he called him out by name. NK [as interpreted] responded and came down to below the house. He talked to Dragan Lukic, who asked him, first of all, how he was, whether he had any problems, and then he asked him where his son was. I don't know what he answered to that, but that conversation lasted some 10 to 20 minutes perhaps. And Dragan Lukic offered VG22 two litres of cognac, a kilo of sugar, or perhaps more, sugar cubes, and some other staples.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: May I stop you there for just a moment, Witness, please. We'll go back to that later on, to that visit by the White Eagles to your brother-in-law, but you said that this group was led by Dragan Lukic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And your brother-in-law, did he know this Dragan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How did he know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: VG22 had a sister, married, in Lukic's village, called Rujiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Your brother-in-law -- is VG22 your brother-in-law, in fact? Will you look at the piece of paper closely, please, the one you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No. No. That's a mistake. He's my sister-in-law -- brother-in-law. My sister is married to VG22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Ossogo, this is a problem with the B/C/S language. Brothers-in-law seems to be a very general phrase which covers a great number of different relationships. But we've now got it that he is the, as I understand it, the husband of his sister-in-law. That may not be right, but you had better just -- if you need to, you better explore it a little bit further and try to avoid the expression "brothers-in-law," because it has such a different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness, this piece of paper has a name, next to which we have said that it was his brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can proceed in this way and then he will be less confused, rather than using the various indications that we have given him. That can cause more confusion. I think he found his way a moment ago, he got it right. Can we continue, Mr. President? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG21, you were telling us the incident that occurred at your brother-in-law's house, and you were saying that Dragan Lukic had taken a certain number of goods, and you were able to identify this brother-in-law because there was an error a moment ago regarding the use of the pseudonym. So let's go back now to Dragan Lukic himself. You have confirmed that he was the one who led the paramilitary group. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No. I saw him only through the curtain of VG22. I was sitting in his house and I was watching him through the window while they were talking outside, and I hadn't known him before then. And that was the first time for me to see him and hear this Dragan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew Milan Lukic, not Dragan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I apologise. That's a mistake. Yes, it was Dragan Lukic, not Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Do you know Mr. Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I know of the name, but I know Sredoje Lukic. I really don't know Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And how did you know Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I know Sredoje because he was a policeman in the town of Visegrad. He performed policemen's duties in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was he present? Was he one of the paramilitary group that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, he was present in the paramilitary units I have mentioned. But just on this occasion, while Dragan Lukic was talking to VG22, I didn't see him. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Talking about VG22, you are really referring to your brother-in-law, aren't you, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about VG22. He is my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is it important in this case? If it is, you had better pursue it, but I suggest we get on to the next matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG21, after all these events that occurred in your brother-in-law's house, did you leave your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I left. I don't know. I think it was the 19th of May, in the morning, together with VG22.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I left my own settlement in the direction of Visegrad. I crossed the bridge on the Drina, not knowing myself where I should go. After everything that had happened that evening in my settlement, where five or six men had gone missing and where Zukic lady was killed -- I can't remember her first name now. She was found in the morning, dead, in her house. She was the wife of Dzemo Zukic. And I went downstream along the Drina in the direction of the town of Zepa because there was no organisation. No one didn't know who to go to or where one would be safe and where one could save one's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So you went to the village of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I was the only one of my family, but with me was VG22, his son, and another neighbour from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you reached Zepa, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I went to my family, because that was where I was born. I was born in Zepa. For the first few days we had no duties or anything in particular to do. Life consisted of struggling for survival and finding enough food to live, for among my immediate family, and I mean my brothers, mother and father, there was no one in the village of Zepa at that point in time, or, rather, the village's name is Pripecak, so that for a couple of days we didn't do anything in particular. There wasn't much shelling. Occasionally there would be a shell or two or some shooting coming from a place called Stolovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: During your stay in Zepa, did you at a certain point in time start hauling bodies out of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: From the River Drina or the lake of Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When was this, if you can remember, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Well, approximately this was the first bodies that appeared, appeared in June, from the 6th of June onwards. From the 12th, their number increased; there were more bodies on the Drina Lake. They came in larger groups from the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us, either approximately or precisely, where you pulled out those bodies? Could you show it to us on a map?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher for his assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Whenever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any issue about this, Mr. Ossogo? Do we need to show it on a map? There was no challenge to the evidence of the previous witness about where the bodies were pulled out from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, indeed, Mr. President. But the map was not used, and it is a complement to the evidence provided in photographs through a previous witness and it allows us to establish the distance from where the points were retrieved to the town of Visegrad, where the bodies were coming from that were thrown into the river. These are just a few additional elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. The witness can't stand up, you realise, because if he does, he loses his facial distortion. That's why I'm curious as to why we have to block everybody's view of this big map. There's a piece of paper floating around. Is this a miniature of the map? I suggest we use that. The witness can show it on the ELMO, and then when the usher has got a moment he can take that down so that the interpreters can see what is going on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I confirm that this is number 149, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is indeed 149, Mr. President. The copy of the map is not clear because it's not in colour, so we're going to use this last document to be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG21, can you see this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I see the map, but I can't really see. I need to look at it a little more closely. The Drina River, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you point, please, to the river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Starting from -- [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
