utterances.text: Yes. Could you pinpoint Visegrad, please, from the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you point to, for the benefit of the Chamber, the area at which you retrieved the bodies in the region of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I can't see very well. I don't have my glasses. But I don't find the map very clear. I'm sorry, I wear glasses, but I don't find the map clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You showed us the river a moment ago, going upstream.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Slap, Slap.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Please look at the point. Show us on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Slap. Pripecak. So it's here. This is the Zepa. Just a moment, please. I'll find it easier on this one. Zepa. Here's the River Zepa. Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG21, this Zepa River, does it flow into the Drina? It joins the Drina some place, at the spot you showed us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. The Zepa flows into the Drina. Yes, here, just here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's sufficient, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in Zepa or, more precisely, in Slap, the place you indicated a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I would go to Slap maybe twice a week to retrieve the bodies from the lake and from the Drina River. Two, three times a week, sometimes not once a week, depending on when I was free. When I was free, I would go almost every day; otherwise, two to three times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, do you want this document, this map, into evidence? It's numbered 149. It's not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, quite. We would like to tender this document as an exhibit, with the number you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P149.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In what condition were the bodies that you retrieved from the Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: The bodies that we retrieved from the Drina Lake were in varying stages of decomposition. Some were whole, intact, some were without heads, without clothing, others were with clothing; younger people, older people, and even children.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you find bodies which were mutilated or that had suffered abuse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. We retrieved bodies which had parts of noses cut off, ears, women with their breasts cut off, then legs tied, naked, both arms slung through the breasts and decomposing. It's indescribable. Some were killed with knives, sledge hammers. I don't know what to say. There were killings of all kind. But in the beginning, bodies mostly arrived that were with a nose cut off, ear cut off, hit with a hammer or a knife. There were few killed with firearms during the first few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Among those bodies, did you find two bodies that were like crucified on a piece of wood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, there were bodies on a door. On one side of the door, a man was nailed to the door and, on the other, a woman. But I personally did not see this, but I was told about this by the person who was in charge of the exhumation or identification of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Who was that person who was in charge of the operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is he a witness or a protected witness? Is the person you seek to obtain from the witness, is he a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not protected, not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, VG21. Who was the person who was in charge of this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: As far as I understand, I am allowed to give the first and last names of the people who were in charge. It was [redacted], also Hamed, I can't just now recollect. Hamed, nicknamed Hodza, was it Bulatovic or -- but I think he had a different surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: He was in charge of doing what? What did [redacted] have as his duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: These two men, with the assistance of the rest of the population of the village of Slap, Pripecak, Zepa, who were not obliged to do work duty or who did not have military duties would assist these two men almost daily, three to four men, maybe more, more out of curiosity, for people to be able to recognise relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, both of you have used the name of a protected witness, and it will be redacted, but please, when we return, make sure that you use the pseudonym. It's quite clear that we will not finish today's evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Which one, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He is the sixth name in the list of protected witnesses that I've got here. But you can check it during the lunch hour. I'm just coming to the point, though, that we are not going to finish the evidence of Mr. Masovic today and we propose to keep sitting tomorrow to take his evidence. At the moment there's nothing listed for tomorrow. Very well. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I checked through the transcript, and (redacted) did give evidence under his own name. So I'm sorry. I'm becoming a little bit edgy about the number of these protected witnesses, but it's perfectly all right. You proceed, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The remark that I wanted to make, and you yourself noted this, was the one you have just made yourself, so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG21, just a few more questions. When you were pulling out the bodies from the river, you distinguished between -- could you distinguish between the men and the women, the male and the female bodies that you pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And you separated the bodies. Did you put them in different graves, depending on the sex? Did you separate the men from the women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, we did dig separately. We put the women in one grave, two or three, depending on how many we pulled out, and we did the same with the men. We would dig special -- we would dig separate graves and bury them in them, depending on how many we pulled out: Three, four, eight, they would all be buried in one grave, depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were there more women than men or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: There were more male bodies pulled out than female ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to determine ethnicity in any way, the ethnicity of the bodies pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. We studied each male body and studied their sexual organs, because Muslim men are circumcised, whereas Orthodox males have different customs and they're not circumcised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: On the basis of that criteria for differentiation, were there bodies which were not Muslim bodies that you pulled out of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I personally didn't see, but I did hear that one body was not circumcised and that that body was pulled out of the Zepa, and we buried -- where we buried the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: On the basis of the bodies you yourself saw, can you confirm that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. All of them except this one body that I didn't see, but I heard from the people who were in charge of that that there was a Serb. One of the bodies belonged to a Serb. He had his driver's licence with him and his ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was there a registry or a way of noting down everything you found on the bodies? Did you record this in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. We had a notebook, an ordinary notebook, and everybody was recorded with a number, from 1 onwards. If it was a female body, we would write "female"; if not, we would write "male," and every object found on them - a watch, a ring - and the clothing that the body was in, we would write down a description of that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these objects that were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: We had a sort of cardboard box, and all the items that we found we would put into a bag or a cardboard box or a suitcase or something like that and take it to the person who had recorded what we had found on the bodies and the bodies themselves, the person in charge of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the notebook where all this was entered into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I personally couldn't say exactly. The best person to give you that kind of information - I don't know if he's protected or not - but (redacted) would be the best man to ask. After the fall of Zepa, he went to Srebrenica, and the notebook was left behind to another person, Amir, nicknamed Hodza. He kept it. Now, what happened later on, where those items were, where they were stored, I really can't tell you anything more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When did you leave Zepa after all these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: In December - I can't remember the exact date, the 6th or the 10th of December, I left the village of Zepa across the territory of the paramilitary units or Serb territory, towards Gorazde. At a place called Crni Vrh, our army was there, that is to say, the Bosnian army, and in December, it was at the Crni Vrh locality in the vicinity of Visegrad. I stayed there with the army for about 10, 15, maybe even 20 days. I can't quite remember all the details, until the first convoy towards Gorazde. From Crni Vrh towards -- going from Crni Vrh towards Gorazde. The journey was a very difficult and risky one because we had to cross mined roads, woods, and territory held by the Serb forces, Serb territory, in fact. After coming to Gorazde and after the several months I spent in Zepa, I found myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness VG22. We have no further questions to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the number of bodies that you succeeded in pulling out of the Drina, but you said that a certain number of bodies went down the river and that you weren't able to retrieve them. Would you be able to say how many bodies escaped you in comparison to the ones that you managed to retrieve? What is the ratio? Would you say you pulled out more bodies or that more bodies got away, so to speak, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The ratio of the bodies and what my associates told me, Hamed, nicknamed Hodza especially, whose job it was to look after that, he said that from the lake formed by the Drina River, 273 bodies were pulled out. However, this probably was in the -- a part from the Visegrad bridge to the dam, and the Muslims tried to pull them out and bury them, give them a proper burial. Of course, it couldn't have been a proper burial, of course, but at least to be able to show that the body had been buried. The number of bodies that disappeared, according to some facts and figures, shows that the number was over 3.000, women, children, men, the elderly and infirm. Over 3.000 that figure is, judging by the census taken in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Persons missing, not bodies. Three thousand persons missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You're talking about the overall number of persons missing, looking at the population census with regard to missing persons for the territory but that's not what I asked you. There are others who were in charge of that. My question was, in relation to those 270-odd bodies which were collected from Visegrad to the place where you were, that is the total number of bodies collected; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No. No. This was what we collected from Visegrad to Perucac and a place called Stolovas and Bajina Basta. But in Slap, as far as I know, and the exhumation that I attended when the bodies were pulled out, I can say that I took out over 60 and buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So this figure represents the number of bodies which from Visegrad, Perucac and Bajina Basta were taken out. But my question to you was: Can you assess the ratio or percentage in relation to the overall number of bodies floating down the Drina River, which might have escaped you and you weren't able to pull them out. Were you able to pull out most of the bodies, a larger portion, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Well, 20, 25 per cent possibly were taken out. Less bodies were taken out and retrieved than the ones that escaped flowing down the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you think that more bodies flowed down the Drina than were pulled out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes, because we did not have the possibility of pulling them out regularly and burying them. The circumstances were such, the conditions in the lake were such that, we couldn't do this. The lake at times -- the water was released at times, and sometimes there was 10, 15 metres of water. The water level changed. Sometimes the bed was dry, so the water level varied, 10, 15 metres, and so on. The other difficulty was the shelling and shooting from small arms from the Starevo village and a hilly place called Stolovas. Everything that moved, whether it was cattle, a cow or a car or whatever, all that was killed. You couldn't be certain of not being hit and not being killed. Everything living was a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the furthest point that the bodies could have flowed down the Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: In my assessment, the town of Visegrad mostly. Most of them came from the town of Visegrad. Because if you look at Fosta [phoen] and Gorazde, well, possibly a body could have crossed the dam, because the water was released, they probably cleaned up there too and buried some bodies, if there were any, or they would let them flow down. Some of the bodies were already decomposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were asked by the -- when you said to the Prosecutor that there was a case of a crucified body on a door, on a plank, you said that you didn't see that personally but you were told this by some other person who was in charge, and you mentioned a name. Could you tell us who told you that exactly? I didn't understand from your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I was referring to Hamed, nicknamed Hodza. And if you're interested, there is proof by people who went to fetch food towards Srebrenica in boats, in the Drina canyon, river canyon, in the rocks there. There were people tied -- who had had their legs tied. I didn't see that, but some living victims -- some living -- some people who survived talked about that, although I don't know whether they're still alive. But two years ago the man was still alive who had seen personally eight people tied together, their legs tied together, eight people in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What I asked you was for that particular case involving Hamed, so it wasn't (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, although they were both in charge, they were in charge of keeping records, and sometimes they both worked together at the same time. Sometimes it was one or the other. But that particular man told me that a man or a woman had been nailed to the door. One person had been nailed to one side of the door, the woman, and the man was nailed to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke of the paramilitary units and where they were stationed in Visegrad, you said that it was the new hotel in Visegrad. My question was whether you meant the Visegrad Hotel, that is to say, the hotel by the famous old bridge. Is that the one you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, when you spoke of your first departure from Visegrad, when you were in Gorazde for nine days, you said today that you did that because of the arrival of the Uzice Corps, which was to have arrived, and you also mentioned the problem with the dam and the water. In the statement you gave to the investigator, you said, and I quote: "I left Visegrad for Gorazde because the dam was opened and we were frightened of flooding. I left on the 13th of April, 1992, and in Visegrad before that there were some political tensions but there weren't any all-out incidents, just general unrest." Is that correct? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's quite true, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And do you maintain that today as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, if I mention the dam and the water, it wasn't a case of -- it was from my personal safety, personal security?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make one request, please, if I may, Your Honours. I should like to correct something that I said. There was some mistakes between Milan and Dragan, when I spoke about Milan and Dragan, so with the Court's indulgence I should like to apologise and say that I had made the -- I had to correct myself, because I got Milan and Dragan mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We understand that, sir. Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. One or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness VG21, at the place where you pulled out the bodies, were you able to estimate the speed of the current, the water current? Was it strong, a strong water current there, or not so strong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: When the lake is closed, shut off, the speed of the water could not be noticed. It flowed by slowly. Then the speed of the water is slow. But when the turbines were working, you could feel that the water was moving more quickly. But as I said a moment ago to Defence counsel, all this depended on how the water from the lake was released. Sometimes it was enough to be released 10 to 15 metres for us not to be able to approach, and sometimes our boats were left on dry land. When the water was not in the lake, the bed was dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Your team, the team that pulled out the bodies, did it work day and night, round the clock, to pull out the bodies that were flowing down the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: No. Just during the day. We worked only during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Very well. So there were bodies floating down the Drina that you could not have seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The mistake you put right with respect to the names you gave, you mixed up the two names. Could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Dragan Savic. He took me to the SUP. He detained me and took me to the SUP, and I have very serious consequences from that. And on one occasion when the accused -- I recognised the accused in the SUP, the police station. The gentleman wanted to interview me with respect to a pistol which Dragan Savic had brought me to the SUP for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I have to stop you there, Witness VG21. You said that you confused two names, so it wasn't -- Dragan Lukic you confused with which other name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: With Dragan Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So you confused Dragan Savic with which other person? What other name did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Milan Lukic. I confused Dragan Savic with Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know those two people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: I don't know Milan Lukic, but I do know Dragan Savic, because on one occasion I saw Milan Lukic out of a window, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You saw him through a window where? Where was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: From the house of VG22.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG22, you mean your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you see what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: He was driving a Passat car. He got out of the car, he talked to the chief. I told you that he gave him two litres of cognac, some oil, some sugar cubes and some other stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did he say anything particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG21
utterances.text: Yes. He told Mr. VG22 not to worry, that he was the chief of the Visegrad SUP, and he gave him the telephone number, his telephone number, if there were any problems, that -- so that he could call him and ask for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, this does not strictly arise out of cross-examination, but you certainly would have leave to deal with it, the witness having drawn attention to the confusion in his mind. But it would have to be subject to further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I have completed my cross-examination [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, do you want to ask any questions arising out of that further material? You may have dealt with it slightly in the course of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That completes your task here. We're grateful to you for having come along to give evidence and for the evidence you gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and I hope that justice will reach every person in the future so that what happened should not happen again. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Masovic is the next witness; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've got the transcript from the Krnojelac case. I've discovered that half of it is put in back to front, but I think I can sort that one out. Is there any -- has there been any suggestion from the Defence that other pages should be added to it, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well, then. Let's have Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you make the solemn declaration in the document which the Court usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Amor Masovic.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Chamber and tell them your name, your current position.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Amor Masovic. By occupation I am a lawyer. Currently I have the position of president of the Federal Commission for the Search of Missing Persons in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina and member of the Commissions for Equality of Sexes and the Administrative Commission of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm also a member of the Auditing Commission of the Association for Criminal Law and Criminology of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. Could you -- I would like to ask you a procedural question. Have you received a copy by way of information of an order of this Chamber issued on the 24th of June, 2001, this year, in which it is indicated that the examination that you will have will not cover a certain number of questions which were covered in another case, that is, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac? Have you been notified or have you received such a document from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You're also aware of the areas that are concerned, the areas we will discuss?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Amor, we have received from you a certain number of documents regarding the very hard work that you have undertaken within the framework of your duties as president or head of the Commission for the Search of Missing Persons, and we're going to work on these documents in the course of this examination-in-chief, for which you have been called here. But first I should like to ask you: In the course of the year 200, and this year, 2001, whether you know exactly how many exhumations have been done within the framework of your activities, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of last year and this current year, in the area of Visegrad municipality or in the environs of Visegrad municipality, 311 victims have been exhumed, out of which 152 have been identified. 159 victims, unfortunately, have still not been identified. These 311 victims were exhumed, if I remember correctly, in 14 different sites, and at some of those sites I was -- I took members of the Commission to visit some of those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a map so that you could give us some information so that the Chamber can see where those sites are. The document is 140-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At some stage, Mr. Ossogo, are you going to tender the transcript of the evidence from the Krnojelac case?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You have there a map containing information on the sites. You mentioned there were 14 in all, as well as the number of bodies which were exhumed at those sites, and the locations, particularly Visegrad, where those exhumations took place. Was this document prepared by you yourself and your service or is it a document coming from a different source?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This document was prepared by my service, specialising in recording and photographing the sites of mass graves, and following my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Very well. Could you, Mr. Amor, show us on this map specifically where the exhumations were done in the area of Slap and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I can point to all the locations. So specifically, if we're talking about Slap, which is close to the settlement of Zepa, we worked on two locations within Slap itself and two locations a little further off having different names. So the first site was Slap 1. It is a site on which one mass grave was discovered with 125 victims buried, sometimes individually, one next to another, and at other times the victims were separate. As for site Slap 2, which is downstream, following the course of the Drina River, or rather, the course of the Perucac Lake, at a distance of about one kilometre from the first site, we found another seven bodies. At site Kamenicko Tocilo, which is situated at about two kilometres from the first site, that is, Slap 1, four victims were found, or, to be more specific, three victims and only parts of a fourth victim, that is, only the skull of that victim was found. And finally, the last site in this region of the Perucac Lake is a site that we have called Luke and which is situated on the right bank of the Drina River, opposite the settlement of Luke, and there three victims were exhumed. All these victims that I have referred to at these four sites, according to sources that we obtained, were people from Visegrad, civilians who were executed in Visegrad and whose bodies flowed down the Drina River and reached these four sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that we can follow this on the transcript later, the sites to which the witness has referred are numbered on this document numbered 140-1. Two, three, four, and five. Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. Those are sites 2, 3, 4, and 5. Add to which a total of 139 victims were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Masovic. You have indicated the position of the various sites where you worked, or rather, your commission, to be able to do the exhumations. Could you tell us, in very general terms: In this particular case, that is, the municipality of Visegrad, which methods did you apply, which systems, in order to achieve these exhumations, on the one hand, and to carry out the identification, on the other, because a moment ago you referred to civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to site number 2, which has officially been named Slap 1, where 125 victims were found, the initial information about the existence of those victims was received by the commission as long ago as 1992. To be more specific, towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, when the first refugees coming from Visegrad and Zepa reached Sarajevo and brought with them reports that along the Drina River a large number of victims had floated as far as the location of Slap, where the local population approached those bodies if they were close to the river bank, without using boats, and if the victims were floating midstream, in the middle of the lake or parallel with the right bank of the River Drina, then the local population used boats to reach those bodies and to transport the bodies to the spot called Slap 1, where these victims were buried. So in fact, the commission has information ever since 1992 about the existence of this mass grave of victims from Visegrad. Witnesses who were refugees from Visegrad and Zepa who brought this information with them spoke about the crimes committed against the civilian, non-Serb population in Visegrad, and as far as I can recall, most of the information had to do with the execution of Visegrad civilians on the spot of two bridges, the old and new bridges in Visegrad, and the victims were liquidated on those very bridges or they were forced to jump alive off the bridge, upon which they were shot at in the water, that is, in the Drina River, while those who were -- until those who were shooting were convinced that the victims were dead. In the course of the war, the Sarajevo commission was unable to undertake any exhumation on this site because the area of Zepa was totally isolated. Actually, it was an enclave within the territory under the control of the forces of Karadzic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. We'll come back to that, Mr. Masovic. So you told us that these were members of the population who came to inform your commission at the head of which you stand, and it was on the basis of that information that you undertook the exhumation. Were they direct witnesses, people who actually experienced the killing or the burying? Were they direct or indirect witnesses? How would you qualify them? How would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The first witnesses who contacted us were probably sort of secondhand witnesses, that is, hearsay witnesses, people who were not directly responsible for the retrieval and burial of the victims. So I'm talking about the witness who came to our commission while the war was still ongoing, that is, the period from 1992 until the end of 1995. Once the war ended, we were also contacted by witnesses who were directly responsible and appointed by the local authorities in Zepa to take care of the retrieval of the victims and to give them a civilised burial, if possible. So these were now first-hand witnesses or eyewitnesses. Specifically, if we're talking about site Slap 2 - so the site marked with the number 3 - we contacted a witness who personally buried those seven victims, which he had, together with another man, pulled out of the Drina River, and in a rather inaccessible part of the river bank, he managed to find a spot where the victims could be buried, which he did. So seven or eight years after the event, that witness personally took us to this site which he was familiar with and he showed us the spot where those seven victims had been buried. As regards site Slap 1, witnesses took us to the actual site and it was visible at first glance already that this was a mass grave, because almost all the victims' graves had been marked with pieces of wood, with ordinal numbers on them, which stood for the victims. At sites 4 and 5, again we were taken there by eyewitnesses who were present when the victims were pulled out of the Drina River and buried on the right bank of that river.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. You yourself, personally, did you participate in detecting those sites once you received the information? Did you have a method or special process of detection after having received this information from witnesses?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call them any special methods; I would call them customary methods used by our commission, and this method, briefly, consists of, wherever possible and whenever eyewitnesses agree, to go on site, together with members of my commission. So that is what we do, that is, we have the eyewitnesses indicate to us the spot. The people in the commission already have a certain amount of experience and they are able to assess whether this is a potential grave, an individual grave, a joint grave or a mass grave or if that is not the case. And in other cases for which we do not have eyewitnesses of the burial of victims, we use some other methods which consist of various examinations of the land, checking the land with the help of mechanical probes or dredgers or backhoes, up to the use of specially trained dogs, trained to discover human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you receive information from other sources, non-local sources which were not dependent upon your commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, from many, many different sources information reached our commission. But when talking about the territory of Visegrad municipality, we had the good fortune of virtually in all cases having eyewitnesses of the events who were able to remember the locations of the individual and mass graves. Only in the case of site Kurtalici, where 62 victims were located, we learnt about the existence of that grave from a Bosniak, a local inhabitant who returned to his home last year after spending eight years as a refugee. And when he went fishing in the lake, he noticed at the very edge of the lake a skeleton, and he didn't know whether it was a human skeleton or not. He contacted our commission and we established that this was a mass grave in which there were 62 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can you give us the exact site when speaking of Kurtalic, when speaking about Kurtalic? Can you give us the exact site?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the site numbered 7, north-west of the town of Visegrad, about ten kilometres away from the centre of Visegrad, downstream, on the right side, or rather, on the right bank of the Perucac Lake or Drina River, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from institutions or international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: I said generally speaking that we receive information from practically all possible sources, and I would like to enumerate as sources, apart from the direct or indirect witnesses, members of their family -- members of the families of the persons missing who have some knowledge about the disappearance of their family members or the liquidation of their family members; next we have reports from our local commissions, which are to be found in different towns throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. In concrete terms, speaking about the Visegrad region, information about what was going on in Visegrad came in from our department or, rather, our regional commission, with its headquarters in the town of Gorazde. Next, we had military sources, police sources, intelligence sources, and sources close to the International Red Cross Committee. In the post-war period, other international organisations such as international police forces, the international police force stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the SFOR, the military force in charge of keeping the peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the office of the High Commissioner and, in the past two years, information has been coming in from the Institute for Missing Persons, with its headquarters in Sarajevo, which was established which the International Commission for Missing Persons, which was set up in 1997, in France, in Lyon, at a meeting of the G7 group and at the initiative of the former president of the United States of America, Mr. Clinton. Therefore, local civilian organs, such as wartime presidencies, they too sent in information about disappearances, the liquidation of persons, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So it is on the basis of all this information that you undertook the exhumations which resulted in the map that you have compiled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way. On the basis of all these sources, all the sources that I mentioned, a database was set up pertaining to persons who had gone missing in the Visegrad area, or rather, further afield in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the course of the war, and that on the basis of direct eyewitnesses as well, except in the Kurtalic case, we went on to the sites, the exhumation sites. And along with standard procedure, we conducted the exhumations themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I should like to go back to the disappearances and exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage we should like to enter into evidence the transcripts which for the moment have the numbers 54/4, and it is the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac. It was in that case. I think you have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's motion for proof of facts, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. We've got that. Is it the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the same. It's quite -- it is the same, one and the same document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the tender of the transcripts, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be Exhibit P54/4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will it be the entire binder that you would like to tender at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've got a limited number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the proceedings, what we could do, Mr. President, is that we indicate that we would like to have this exhibit tendered into evidence from the registrar, from the binder, and then we can go on to adopting it later on in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At the moment, though, you are dealing only with material that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we will leave it with the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At the moment you are dealing only with the material that was attached to the motion under Rule 92 bis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that is, as I say, Exhibit P54/4 you can sort out with the deputy later on what part of the folder that comprises and we'll deal with the rest of it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Amor, can we move on to the practical details? You said that you were present at the exhumations yourself; is that right? For all the exhumations, but in particular for the Visegrad exhumations, you were present yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: At some of the exhumations I was present myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you present at the Slap 1?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Slap 1 and Slap 2 sites, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you were able to compile a report or establish a link? Do you follow my question? Could you tell us if you established -- there was a report or any documents relative to the Slap 1 and 2 exhumation sites?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The victims reached the locality, the site, Slap 1 and 2, in almost the same manner. They were victims, and this was shown during the identification process. Some of the victims that we found at the Slap 1 site who were liquidated some 25 or more kilometres upstream, that is to say, in the town of Visegrad. they were thrown into the Drina River then, and the River Drina brought those victims downstream to the territory of the town of Zepa and the Slap site, which was under the control of government forces, and where the local population from Zepa, just like the inhabitants of Visegrad, who had succeeded on leaving Visegrad in time, pulled out those bodies to the bank and buried them there. And there is no difference between sites 2, 3, 4, and 5 when it comes to the way in which -- or rather, how the victims came to find themselves in that locality. All the victims were brought down by the Drina River, flowed down the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I was just asking you whether you had established any documents with respect to the exhumations you conducted at the Slap sites. Now, I have a document here and I'd like to have your opinion on it. I'd like to ask you some questions with respect to those exhumations. They refer to Slap sites 1 and 2. It is Exhibit 54/5, table B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this the balance of the binder which is labelled Exhibit 54?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 54/5, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, this is new. I'm not complaining, but I just want to make sure we understand what we've got here now. This document, this folder which is labelled 54, comprises 54/1, which we haven't seen in evidence yet, 54/2, which we haven't seen, 54/3, which we haven't seen. Now, 54.5 is what you're dealing with now. I'm sorry. We have seen 54.4, which is at the back, I think. Yes. So we'll use this folder bearing in mind that you will eventually get the whole -- or be tendering the whole of it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: The document entitled "Table B" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, Table B.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: This document with that title was compiled by the Commission for the Quest of Missing Persons of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation, and in that document, that is to say, the document contains 152 names of persons who were exhumed at 14 different sites in the Visegrad municipality or the environs of Visegrad municipality, of the 311 victims who were exhumed. I said in my introduction that there were 311 victims and 152 were identified, and their names, first and last names, are contained in the document titled "Table B." From the table, you can see, if that is at all important, if you're interested in it, and I think it could be important, that victim 41, for example, victim number 41, was a female. Her name was Hanka Halilovic. She was born in 1900, and at the moment of liquidation in 1992 she was 92 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Masovic. Let me just stop you for a minute. The document that you refer to, Table B, comprises two annexes, annex 1 and annex 2. Those two annexes, annex 1 and 2, are they annexes which provide us with more details of the map which was compiled by your commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These two documents tabled B, annex 1 and annex 2, are textual descriptions of the map, which was compiled by my commission, and in annex 1, for example, we enumerate all 14 sites relating to exhumation in the Visegrad municipality in the period between the year 2000 and 2001. And the annex 2 table enumerates those same sites, that is to say, the 14 sites, but they were grouped either according to the geographical location or the time at which the events took place, time in which the events took place. So that those 14 sites are divided into three areas, three regions, and this can be seen on the map itself. Those three areas have been marked site 1, with only one locality of exhumation; then we have area 2, where we have four sites, Slap 1, Slap 2, Kamenicko Tocilo, and Luke; and the third area, where we have nine different sites where exhumations were conducted. They are Kurtalici 1 and 2, Balimo [phoen], Gornja Mostanica, Crni Vrh, Jelacici, and Visegrad. So these names are in fact the names of the villages surrounding the urban part of the town of Visegrad, villages in which the exhumations were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The circles on the map, there are three big circles, a big one, medium sized one and a small one, and the numbers are 1, 2, and 3; do they correspond to what is contained in annex 2 of table B? Let's take group 1. Does that correspond to the first circle and the group 2 to the second circle and group 3 to the third circle on the map? Do they correspond?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I've just been explaining. They are three groups, or three areas which are textually described in annex 2. They contain the name of the locality, the number of victims exhumed, the number of victims identified, and the number of non-identified victims in each of the localities, on each of the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: To go back to Table B proper, and we see several columns there: Name, father's name, et cetera, columns, date of birth, first name, date of birth, sex, and present residence, the address of the person whose body was found. We see that in annex 1 of Table B we have the number of identified. Was it the identification number of the person or -- actually, can you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: We have here a number, the mathematical expression of the number of exhumed victims. If, for example, in annex 1 we have the Kalimanici site, Yama Paklenik, then the next column denotes the number of victims found and exhumed, and that was 73. After that, you have the number of identified victims, how many victims were identified, and that was 65, 65 victims were identified. And then the next column denotes the number of unidentified victims, and there were eight of those. And finally, the last column shows the group in which this locality is to be found; group 1, 2, or 3, which are marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. To go back to the observations, there's a column where it says "sex" on Table B, the main table, Table B, and you've just told us that there are two columns in the annex, in annex 1 of Table B, which indicates the people exhumed, identified, and unidentified. Could you tell the Chamber how you proceeded to the identification process. Do you make a difference between exhumation and the identification of those people? How did you identify them? Did you determine what shape the bodies were in, whether they were male, female, and what shape the bodies were in?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: An autopsy of the victims is the method in which we establish the sex of the victim, so autopsy and forensic expertise, determines whether the victim is male or female. When I say "identification," we just determine the identity of the victim, which means their first and last names. And from Table B, we can ascertain that of the 311 victims which we succeeded in finding and exhuming, 152 have been identified up until the present day. The remaining 159 victims have still not been identified, although their sex was determined; we know whether they were men or women. So although we know their sex, we don't know who they are. Of the 159 victims, we took samples of their skeletons and we are in the process of doing DNK or DNA analyses using the blood of potential relatives and bone samples as well in order to establish the identity of the remaining 159 men and women who are as yet unidentified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: As regards names, the names indicated on Table B, in view of the fact that you have given us explanations with respect to sex determination, which is a start for identifying the individuals as such, can you explain how you were able to establish, for example, number 2, that it was in fact Emin Hadzic [phoen], whose father's name was Fadil? Were they direct -- did you get this information from direct eyewitnesses or indirect witnesses or how did you establish the actual names, the identities?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, in some of the cases we had information that at a certain time, in a certain place, such-and-such a person or so many people had been liquidated, and they state -- and the names and -- the first names and last names of the victims were stated. Let me give you an example, a possible example. Let's say that the event took place in Visegrad, on the bridge, that they were executed, that is to say, five men were executed on a certain day in the month of June, 1992, and one day or two days later, or a few hours after the event, the river Drina brings with it to the Slap site the bodies of victims which the local inhabitants are able to recognise. On the Slap site, therefore, a list was compiled of some 50 names of the 125, which was the total number of bodies pulled out of the Drina. So some 50 of these names, the local population was able to identify while the bodies were being pulled out of the Drina River. The local inhabitants recognised them. Of course, the commission for the identification of victims, which was made up of the judge of the cantonal court, the Prosecutor, the crime technician policeman, and the physician, or rather, the forensic expert who is a doctor, medical doctor by profession, would need a little more in order to determine the identity of each and every victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's 4.00. The Court will break now. We'll resume again tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to ask you, if possible, to begin somewhat later tomorrow. For example, at 10.00. I thought we would have a free day tomorrow and I have some duties to attend to at the airport tomorrow morning. So may I beg the Court's indulgence and ask that we begin at 10.00 a.m. I hope we have only Mr. Masovic and I hope to get through him in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean you'll be back from the airport by 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right. I see Mr. Masovic is put down for a three-hour hearing. I hope we'll be able to contain it within that -- we've got a little more time to manoeuvre, but I would like to finish him tomorrow. That's all. So perhaps that would keep some sort of a brake upon excess cross-examination, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of September, 2001, at 10.00 a.m.
